cf.title: [PATCH v1 0/7] Wait event timing and tracing instrumentation

input.subject: [PATCH v1 0/7] Wait event timing and tracing instrumentation

verdict_reasoning: The series fails at level 1b, so the design objections are not ranked. Messages #13 and #18 ask to settle first whether core observes waits by sampling, at selected sites, or at every transition, and the thread shows no agreement (maintenance-fit-4). Message #19 reproduces the main result with an external tracer on stock PG18, so the shown gain is lower cost and no host access (already-exists-2). The proposal does not say why the collector must be in contrib (already-exists-1).

brief.title: Timed wait event hooks with a contrib module for wait timing and tracing
brief.problem: Postgres shows wait events in pg_stat_activity only as snapshots, so users cannot see how long backends spend in each wait or the order of a session's waits. Sampling tools such as pg_wait_sampling miss short waits and cannot rebuild one slow request. The target users are DBAs who are diagnosing incidents.
brief.proposed_design: The current series (v14) adds wait_event_begin_hook and wait_event_end_hook, called from a new pair pgstat_report_wait_start_timed()/pgstat_report_wait_end_timed(), and converts all 94 core wait sites to the timed pair. A new module, contrib/pg_wait_event_tracing, uses the hooks to keep per-backend statistics (count, total, max, histogram) and a per-session trace ring with query-attribution markers. The first version (v1 to v6) did this in core behind a configure flag.
user_visible_surface: C API: wait_event_begin_hook, wait_event_end_hook, pgstat_report_wait_start_timed(), pgstat_report_wait_end_timed(), and a documented hook contract
New contrib extension pg_wait_event_tracing, which must be in shared_preload_libraries
GUC pg_wait_event_tracing.capture (off | stats | trace, SUSET), plus two other module GUCs
SQL views and functions for statistics, resets, capacity, orphaned-ring cleanup and the trace ring
pg_wait_event_trace_by_statement(), which groups waits by statement and returns a phase column and <idle>/<no-statement> buckets
author_claims: With no consumer loaded, the timed pair adds about 2 ns per wait pair on an already-set latch and no resolved end-to-end TPS difference.
With capture on, a lock-heavy workload loses about 3.3% TPS and other pgbench workloads lose up to about 1%.
Exact per-wait timing explained a slow-request tail in a test where pg_wait_sampling pointed to the wrong waits.
Timing only some wait sites would leave unexplained gaps, so the author converts all sites.
Guillaume Lelarge and Kirk Wolak say the feature is useful.
brief.thread_state: Andres Freund is "dead set against" the hooks, objects to converting every wait site, and prefers a configurable wait event sampler; the author answered but kept all sites converted. Michael Paquier and Andrey Borodin raised cost and observation-contract concerns, and no committer supports the current shape.
unclear: The material does not show any committer accepting a hook on all wait sites, or saying which sites, if any, may use the timed pair.
The v14 overhead numbers come from v11; the author has not re-run them for v12 to v14.
The material does not say how the hook contract (no palloc, locks, waits or errors) is enforced for third-party consumers beyond documentation.
The material does not say whether the module stays in contrib or moves out of tree if the hook is accepted.

prior_attempts.title: Add accumulated statistics for wait event
prior_attempts.who_objected: Michael Paquier, Kyotaro Horiguchi, Daniel Gustafsson
prior_attempts.quote: Since the thread has stalled and there is no updated patch I've marked this entry Returned with Feedback.
prior_attempts.reason: The patch stopped applying to HEAD. The author said there was no time to rebase it in that commitfest, so the entry was returned with feedback. Earlier, Michael Paquier argued that client-side sampling of pg_stat_activity finds bottlenecks at lower cost than server-side counters for all backends. Benchmarks showed up to about 10% overhead in read-only tests, and Kyotaro Horiguchi found frequent hash lookups even with timing off.
prior_attempts.what_is_different: P3 kept per-backend wait counts and accumulated times in core with a hash table and a track_wait_timing setting. This series moves collection to a contrib module behind hooks, adds a trace ring with statement attribution, and reports about 2 ns of cost with no consumer loaded.

objections.title: Every-transition observation chosen before the observation contract is agreed
objections.failure_scenario: Core commits hooks on every wait transition. Later the project adds the configurable sampler Andres describes, and then has two overlapping wait observation mechanisms. The hooks cannot be removed without breaking extensions that came to depend on them.
objections.argument: Message #13 asks to settle first whether the contract is sampling, selected extended sites, or every transition. Message #18 rejects the premise that wait timing alone is useful and prefers sampling with state context. The overhead figures in message #19 come from v11, and v12 to v14 were not measured again. A hook API offered to extensions is hard to withdraw once it ships.
objections.author_must_show: Why should core commit permanent every-transition hooks before the project agrees whether a sampler would answer the same incident questions?

critic.reasoning: Message #13 asks to settle the observation contract first, and message #18 prefers a sampler; the thread shows no agreement. Hooks can change between major releases, so the regret is smaller than stated, but the open question stands.

objections.title: Exact per-wait timing is already possible on stock builds
objections.failure_scenario: A DBA who can run eBPF on the host already gets exact per-wait durations from my_wait_event_info on an unpatched server, as the author did on stock PG18. The proposal adds a permanent API and 94 converted sites, and its added value is lower cost per transition and use without host access.
objections.argument: Message #19 reproduces the main result, Lock:transactionid dominating slow requests, with an external eBPF tracer on stock PG18. Message #1 gives that tracer's cost as about 200-300 ns per transition. So the gap is overhead and deployment, and is not capability. Users on managed services still depend on the provider loading the module, so the hook does not by itself close the deployment gap.
objections.author_must_show: Which incident could not be diagnosed with the existing external tracer plus pg_wait_sampling, track_io_timing and log_lock_waits, and why is the cost difference decisive?

critic.reasoning: Message #19 reproduces the main result with an external eBPF tracer on stock PG18, so the gap is cost and host access. The thread shows two short supporting replies and no field reports from users who cannot use that tracer.

objections.title: Collector module belongs out of tree once the hook exists
objections.failure_scenario: A future patch changes protocol handling, the executor hooks or transaction callbacks. The contrib module's statement-attribution state machine silently misplaces waits, and the committer who touched postgres.c now owns fixing a module they never reviewed. Users find out when pg_wait_event_trace_by_statement() puts lock waits in the wrong bucket.
objections.argument: Patches 0004 and 0005 are about 480 KiB and use only the hook from 0001 plus existing extension hooks. pg_wait_sampling already shows that a wait collector can be maintained out of tree. In message #13, Andrey suggested a small core hook with a separately maintained collector, and the proposal does not say why contrib placement is needed. Message #16 already lists four ambiguous attribution cases.
objections.author_must_show: What does contrib placement give pg_wait_event_tracing that an out-of-tree extension using the same hook cannot have?

critic.reasoning: Message #13 notes the deployment value of in-tree diagnostics, but the same message proposes a small core hook with a separately maintained collector. The proposal does not say what contrib placement adds over that.

other_surviving.title: Converts all wait sites, where earlier discussion allowed only selected ones
other_surviving.failure_scenario: A developer adds a wait event deep in the I/O or lock path and uses the timed pair, as the new xfunc text recommends for new code. Any loaded consumer now runs arbitrary code at that site, which nobody analysed for this site. The regression or misbehaviour shows up in the field, under the hook contract that nothing enforces.
other_surviving.argument: The earlier wait-event statistics thread allowed explicit per-site opt-in, with each conversion reasoned about or measured. The author summarizes it that way in message #7, Michael Paquier points to it in message #6, and Andres Freund restates it in message #18 ("*some* cases ... one-by-one analysis"). v14-0002 converts all 94 starts and their 111 end and cleanup calls, so the per-site split exists only in name. Message #19 keeps all sites for the use case, but that rebuilds the shape the earlier discussion ruled out.
other_surviving.author_must_show: Which individual wait sites justify the timed pair on their own analysis, and would the use case still hold if only those were converted?

critic.reasoning: Message #18 accepts only some sites with one-by-one analysis, and message #19 keeps all 94 converted. The 2 ns null-hook measurement answers the run-time cost, but it does not answer the per-site analysis or the code-size objection.

other_surviving.not_ranked_reason: level 2 is above the failing level 1b: not evaluated (base-up stop rule)

other_surviving.title: A second wait-reporting pair splits one API into two
other_surviving.failure_scenario: A developer adds a wait site in core or in an extension and picks pgstat_report_wait_start() out of habit. No build error or test failure follows. A DBA using pg_wait_event_tracing later sees that wait counted as un-waited time inside a slow request, and the profile points to the wrong cause.
other_surviving.argument: Postgres has one verb for reporting a wait. v14-0001 adds a second pair with the same calling convention, and v14-0002 moves all 94 core sites to it, so the old pair stays only as a trap for new code. The xfunc.sgml hunk tells add-ins to prefer the timed pair and to wrap calls in a PG_VERSION_NUM check. In message #18 Andres Freund accepted at most a per-site opt-in with analysis for each site, and objected to the conversion of all sites.
other_surviving.author_must_show: If every core site uses the timed pair, why keep two public reporting pairs, and what makes a new site that uses the wrong one fail loudly?

critic.reasoning: The material shows no check that fails when a new site uses the ordinary pair, so the trace loses that wait silently. A new version could convert fewer sites or keep one pair, so the severity is fixable.

other_surviving.not_ranked_reason: level 2 is above the failing level 1b: not evaluated (base-up stop rule)

other_surviving.title: Contrib functions take names from the core pg_stat_ namespace
other_surviving.failure_scenario: A later release adds a core wait-event view or reset function, such as the sampler suggested in message #18, under a pg_stat_*wait_event* name. A cluster that has the extension installed then fails pg_upgrade or the restore of a dump with a duplicate-function error. Users also cannot tell which functions are core and which belong to the module.
other_surviving.argument: v14-0004 and v14-0005 ship pg_stat_reset_wait_event_timing(), pg_stat_reset_wait_event_timing_all() and pg_stat_clear_orphaned_wait_event_rings() from contrib. These names were core names in v1-v6. Contrib modules normally prefix their objects with the module name, for example pg_stat_statements_reset(). Here the module prefix is used for some objects and not for others.
other_surviving.author_must_show: Why do the module's reset and cleanup functions keep core-style pg_stat_ names, when they could use the pg_wait_event_tracing_ prefix that the other module functions use?

critic.reasoning: The 0004 and 0005 commit messages name pg_stat_reset_wait_event_timing() and pg_stat_clear_orphaned_wait_event_rings() beside module-prefixed functions. The duplicate-function error is unlikely, because extension functions live outside pg_catalog, but a later core function of the same name would shadow them.

other_surviving.not_ranked_reason: level 2 is above the failing level 1b: not evaluated (base-up stop rule)

other_surviving.title: Orphaned trace rings stay in DSA until a superuser sweeps them
other_surviving.failure_scenario: During an incident a DBA runs alter system to set capture = trace with the default ring size of about 4 MiB, while a pooler churns hundreds of sessions. Capture is then set back to off. Each exited session leaves an orphaned ring, successors that do not trace never reclaim it, and the DSA memory stays allocated until someone runs pg_stat_clear_orphaned_wait_event_rings().
other_surviving.argument: The 0005 commit message says a ring is orphaned on process exit and reclaimed only when a later session attaches on the same ProcNumber, or by the superuser-only sweep. Message #1 already lists orphan retention as an open trade-off. The material shows no cap on total orphaned memory and no automatic expiry. So the worst case scales with max_connections times the ring size.
other_surviving.author_must_show: What bounds the total memory held by orphaned rings when capture is turned off cluster-wide, and what frees it without a manual superuser call?

critic.reasoning: The 0005 commit message frees an orphaned ring only when a tracing successor attaches on the same ProcNumber or a superuser runs the sweep. The total is bounded by max_connections times ring size, which can reach GiB, and message #1 leaves this trade-off open.

other_surviving.not_ranked_reason: level 2 is above the failing level 1b: not evaluated (base-up stop rule)

other_surviving.title: Hook contract is unenforced in critical sections and during release
other_surviving.failure_scenario: A third-party consumer calls palloc or takes an LWLock in wait_event_end_hook. Under load, a backend that is inside a critical section or releasing its resource owner hits a FATAL or PANIC. The user reports it as a core crash in lwlock.c or fd.c.
other_surviving.argument: Message #9 showed this failure mode in the patch's own collector, where an on-demand attach during resource-owner release caused ResourceOwnerEnlarge to fail. The contract (no palloc, locks, waits or errors) exists only as documentation. The test_wait_hook README states that the depth guard leaves the outer wait reading stale state. Core would carry an API whose misuse shows up far from its cause, and whose triage would fall on core committers.
other_surviving.author_must_show: What does core check at run time, at least under assertions, so that a hook that allocates, locks or errors fails at the hook rather than as an unrelated crash?

critic.reasoning: Message #9 shows the collector itself hit this failure during resource-owner release, and the contract is documentation only. Assert builds catch palloc in a critical section today, but nothing catches a lock or an error raised in a hook.

other_surviving.not_ranked_reason: level 2 is above the failing level 1b: not evaluated (base-up stop rule)

refuted.title: By-statement attribution is a heuristic exposed as a stable SQL result
refuted.failure_scenario: A DBA builds alerts on pg_wait_event_trace_by_statement() phase and bucket values. A minor release fixes one of the four documented ambiguous cases, such as pipelined Parse messages. The same workload then reports different per-statement wait totals, and the alert history stops matching.
refuted.argument: Message #16 changed the bucket rules, added the phase column and added the <no-statement> bucket after the v11 rules attributed lock-convoy waits to <idle>. The documentation still lists four cases where attribution is ambiguous, and message #19 says the in-transaction ClientRead split was done outside the function. A contrib SQL function is a user-facing contract, and fixes to its rules change the results users already rely on.
refuted.author_must_show: How will later changes to the attribution rules be versioned, so that results from one release can be compared with results from the next?

critic.reasoning: The function reads a fixed-size ring that is overwritten, and the documentation lists the four ambiguous cases. Contrib functions change results between extension versions today, and Postgres minor releases do not usually change such rules.

refuted.title: Timed hooks run inside WAL and control file critical sections
refuted.failure_scenario: A third-party timing consumer calls palloc or elog in its end hook. A backend flushes WAL in XLogFlush, or the checkpointer writes pg_control through update_controlfile(), inside a critical section, and the hook fires there. The error turns into a PANIC and the whole cluster restarts; on a standby, the startup process stops replay the same way.
refuted.argument: Patch 0002 converts every site, including xlog.c, the WAL writer, standby.c, the startup process paths and the two update_controlfile() sites. Patch 0001 makes the no-palloc, no-lock, no-error contract a documentation rule, and the test module shows that the depth guard only blocks re-entry. Andres Freund objects to running arbitrary code at all wait sites in message #18. Message #19 keeps all sites converted, so the durable-state paths carry the same hook as cheap waits.
refuted.author_must_show: Which converted sites run inside a critical section or hold ControlFileLock or WALWriteLock, and why must a third-party hook run at those sites rather than leaving them on the ordinary pair?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of maintenance-fit-2. Both describe a third-party hook that breaks the documented contract in a critical section; the per-site question is covered by prior-attempts-1.

refuted.title: Converting all 94 wait sites makes every wait site a hook site
refuted.failure_scenario: A developer adds a wait event deep in the I/O or lock path, possibly inside a critical section. If they use the ordinary pair, pg_wait_event_tracing silently loses that time and nothing fails. If they use the timed pair, they place arbitrary extension code there, and no test or review rule tells them which choice is correct.
refuted.argument: Patch 0002 moves every direct wait site to the timed pair, and the xfunc.sgml hunk tells add-ins to prefer the timed pair for new code. This leaves two reporting APIs that every future wait site must choose between. In message #18 Andres rejects both the hook on all wait sites and the code-size growth at each site. Message #19 keeps all sites converted, and no committer has accepted that.
refuted.author_must_show: Which wait sites, analysed one by one, justify the timed pair, and what rule tells future authors which pair a new wait event must use?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of prior-attempts-1 for the conversion of all sites, and of standards-compat-1 for the choice between two pairs. It adds no separate point, and its fatal severity does not hold because converting fewer sites is possible.

refuted.title: Large contrib collector with no committer taking ownership
refuted.failure_scenario: A future change to DSA, ProcNumber reuse, auxiliary process startup, or protocol message handling breaks the module's lock-free slot claiming, seqlock rings, orphan sweep or statement attribution. A core committer who never reviewed about 480 KiB of patches and a 1,600-line SGML page then has to diagnose it.
refuted.argument: Patches 0004 and 0005 add a lock-free fixed region for auxiliary processes, owner tokens, per-session DSA rings with post-mortem reads, and a statement-attribution state machine whose documentation already lists four ambiguous cases. In message #13 Borodin proposed a small core hook and a separately maintained extension. The brief notes that the material does not say whether the module stays in contrib. Only non-committers support the feature in the thread.
refuted.author_must_show: Which committer will own contrib/pg_wait_event_tracing, and why must it live in contrib rather than outside the tree on top of a minimal hook?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of already-exists-1 for the contrib placement. The missing committer owner belongs in the committability field, and the rubric says it must not raise the verdict.

refuted.title: Exact per-wait timing already works on stock Postgres via external tracing
refuted.failure_scenario: A DBA with a slow-request tail can attach an eBPF tracer to stock Postgres and rebuild requests from exact waits, as message #19 did on PG18. The project takes on a hook contract, 94 converted sites and a large contrib module for a group that already has a working tool.
refuted.argument: Message #19 confirms the slow-request diagnosis with an external eBPF tracer on unpatched PG18, getting 75% against the patch's 65%. Outside the author, the only demand in the thread is two short replies (messages #5 and #12), and message #1 credits Kirk Wolak as a tester. Message #13 notes that diagnostics missing on managed installs are of little use, but a module that needs shared_preload_libraries also depends on the provider. Precedent [P3] asked for similar accumulated wait timing and did not get in.
refuted.author_must_show: Which users cannot use eBPF or sampling today but could load this module, and do field reports from them exist beyond this thread?

precedents.title: Add accumulated statistics for wait event

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of already-exists-2. P3 must not be used as support: it was returned because the patch stalled without a rebase and showed about 10% overhead, which says nothing about demand here.

refuted.title: Cost of converting every wait site falls on all users
refuted.failure_scenario: Each future patch that adds a wait site must choose between the plain and timed pairs and respect a hook contract in deep contexts. All builds carry the larger code at 94 sites, while only clusters that preload the collector gain anything.
refuted.argument: Message #18 objects to the larger code at every wait site and to running arbitrary code there. Message #6 warns that adding wait events becomes harder to reason about. The author keeps all sites converted because partial coverage leaves gaps (message #19), so the shared cost stays tied to the full set. The thread shows no user group large enough to outweigh a cost that every backend pays.
refuted.author_must_show: Which specific wait sites have users who need exact timing, and why can the rest not stay on the plain pair?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of prior-attempts-1 for the choice at each new wait site and the code size. For the run-time part, messages #14 and #15 measure about 2 ns per pair with no consumer and no resolved TPS difference.

touch_points.label: WAL / replication / standby
touch_points.reason: v14-0002 converts wait sites in xlog.c, walwriter, walsender, walreceiver and standby.c to the hooked pair; no WAL format change.

touch_points.label: ABI / extension API
touch_points.reason: v14-0001 adds wait_event_begin_hook, wait_event_end_hook and a second public reporting pair with a documented hook contract.

touch_points.label: new GUC
touch_points.reason: The module adds pg_wait_event_tracing.capture and two other GUCs.

touch_points.label: security / privileges
touch_points.reason: SUSET capture GUC, cross-backend trace reads by pg_read_all_stats, and reset functions with pg_signal_backend-style checks.

touch_points.label: maintenance burden ("who maintains this in 10 years")
touch_points.reason: Every future wait site must choose between two pairs, and contrib gains a large collector tied to executor and protocol hooks.

touch_points.label: performance on the hot path
touch_points.reason: All 94 wait sites, including LWLock, spinlock and I/O waits, gain a hook pointer test.

touch_points.label: doesn't fit what Postgres is about (extension / external tool / already solved)
touch_points.reason: Message #13 suggests a small core hook with the collector maintained outside the tree; an external eBPF tracer gives exact timing today.

questions: Why should core add hooks on every wait transition before the list agrees whether a configurable sampler answers the same incident questions?
Which incident could not be diagnosed with the external eBPF tracer plus pg_wait_sampling, track_io_timing and log_lock_waits, and why is the cost difference decisive?
What does contrib placement give pg_wait_event_tracing that an out-of-tree extension using the same hook cannot have?
Which individual wait sites justify the timed pair on their own analysis, and does the use case still hold if only those are converted?
What are the no-consumer and capture-on overhead numbers when measured on v14 instead of v11?

committability.owner_note: Andres Freund and Michael Paquier take part in the thread, but Andres Freund opposes the hooks and no committer supports the current shape. The owner would need to know the wait event, LWLock and I/O paths.
committability.liability: The owner signs for a hook at every wait site, including sites inside critical sections, with a contract that only documentation enforces. The owner also signs for a large contrib module whose statement attribution depends on executor, protocol and transaction hooks, for as long as it ships.
committability.author_follow_up: The author posted 14 versions in about four months and answered each review, which suggests the author stays for fixes.

priority.reason: The goal has support from DBAs in the thread, but the series converts 94 sites and adds about 480 KiB of contrib patches while a committer who knows the area opposes hooks on all sites. Agreement on sampling, selected sites or every transition must come before code review.

provisional_note: No code was read. The cost with no consumer loaded, the code-size growth at each site, and the safety of the lock-free slot claiming and the seqlock ring could not be judged; the level 2 objections were not evaluated.
disclosure: Prepared by an AI harness; treat as a devil's advocate, not a verdict.

precedents_retrieved.title: Add new wait event to XactLockTableWait
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds a wait event, first WAIT_EVENT_XACT_DONE and later WAIT_EVENT_XACT_COMPLETE, which XactLockTableWait() and ConditionalXactLockTableWait() report during their pg_usleep() calls. Backends in these waits, for example while creating a logical replication slot on a busy system, then show a wait event in pg_stat_activity instead of NULL.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The visible messages do not show why. Fujii Masao and Dilip Kumar approved v3, the author marked it Ready for Committer, and Fujii Masao said he would commit it once v19 development opened. No objection appears, and the thread ends in June 2025 while the entry was withdrawn in March 2026.

precedents_retrieved.title: Fix cleanup of WSA events in WIN32 wait event code
precedents_retrieved.summary: Fix cleanup of WSA events in WIN32 wait event code

precedents_retrieved.title: Add accumulated statistics for wait event
precedents_retrieved.objectors: Michael Paquier, Kyotaro Horiguchi, Daniel Gustafsson
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch records, per backend and per wait event, the number of waits and the accumulated wait time, so the counts survive after the wait ends and appear in a view such as pg_stat_waitaccum. Later versions keep these statistics in a hash table and add a track_wait_timing setting to turn the timing part on and off.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The patch stopped applying to HEAD. The author said there was no time to rebase it in that commitfest, so the entry was returned with feedback. Earlier, Michael Paquier argued that client-side sampling of pg_stat_activity finds bottlenecks at lower cost than server-side counters for all backends. Benchmarks showed up to about 10% overhead in read-only tests, and Kyotaro Horiguchi found frequent hash lookups even with timing off.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
Since the thread has stalled and there is no updated
patch I've marked this entry Returned with Feedback.

precedents_retrieved.title: pg_stat_activity: avoid showing state=active with wait_event=ClientRead
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch makes pg_stat_activity read each backend's state and wait event in one pass, so active backends no longer show wait_event ClientRead under high load. It also changes how the local copy of backend status is allocated, using chunks instead of one allocation sized by max_connections.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Robert Haas argued that the state and the wait event are set by different functions at different times, so any reader can see them out of step and the patch can only narrow the race. He said these lightweight introspection views were never meant to be consistent with each other, and that making them so would add complexity and slow the system down. The thread ends with the authors asking for the patch plus a documentation note, and no reply is shown.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
The very best a patch like this can hope to do is narrow the
race condition enough that the discrepancies are observed less
frequently in practice.

precedents_retrieved.title: Fix Windows network event handling
precedents_retrieved.summary: On Windows, the patch moves socket event handles out of each WaitEventSet into a reference-counted per-socket hash table, and adds its own level-triggered event memory, so the edge-triggered FD_CLOSE event is no longer lost. It also changes simplehash for raw malloc/free and no-OOM behaviour, and would let the graceful socket shutdown on Windows be put back.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The entry was returned with feedback in the 2024-01 commitfest because CFbot showed test failures and no updated version followed. In review, Robert Haas questioned the simplehash changes: whether SH_RAW_FREE is needed, whether the no-OOM change in 0002 is a good idea at all, and why raw malloc/free is used instead of palloc/pfree. The visible messages show no reply to that review.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: I wonder whether we really want 0002. It seems like a pretty significant behavior change -- now everybody using simplehash has to worry about whether failure cases are possible.

precedents_retrieved.title: Xact event callback at command start
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds a way for an extension to run code before each SQL statement in a transaction, so that it can implement server-side statement-level rollback. Early versions used hooks around start_xact_command(), later versions used a new XACT_EVENT_COMMAND_START event for xact callbacks, and v5 went back to a hook called after start_xact_command().
precedents_retrieved.objection: Andres Freund and Tom Lane objected to exposing an API for statement-level rollback in an extension, because top-level transaction state is tied to backend internals and the hook placements would be fragile and add overhead to the exec_* functions in postgres.c. Andres Freund added that a real solution needs core work, such as making subtransactions cheap enough to avoid xid wraparound, and that these hooks do not move toward it. Tom Lane also said the new xact callback events were the wrong design, since they broke postgres_fdw. After this, the author said there was no chance of inclusion and offered to withdraw the patch.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: I'm *very* unconvinced it makes sense to implement a feature like this in an extension / that we should expose API for that purpose. To me the top-level transaction state is way too tied to our internals for it to be reasonably dealt with in an extension.

precedents_retrieved.objection:
This reverts commit b860848232aa, that was added as a prerequisite for
the support of pgstats data flush across checkpoints, linking a pgstats
file to a specific checkpoint redo LSN.

As reported, this is proving to be currently problematic when going
through a pg_upgrade, that does direct manipulations of the control file
in the new cluster.  The LSN stored in the pgstats file is not able to
cope with any changes done in the control file by pg_upgrade yet,
causing the pgstats file to be discarded when starting the new cluster
after overriding its redo LSN (one is a `pg_resetwal -l` where the new
cluster's start LSN is bumped by a hardcoded value of 8 segments, see
copy_xact_xlog_xid).

The least painful path going forward is likely going to be a refactor of
the pgstats code so as it is possible to read and write some of its data
with some routines in src/common/, so as pg_upgrade or pg_resetwal are
able to update its data.  The main point is that we are going to need a
LSN in the stats file should we make it written at checkpoint time and
not only as part of a shutdown sequence.  It is too late to dive into
these details for v18, so let's revert the change, and let's try to
figure out all the details in the next release cycle.  The pgstats file
is currently only written as part of a shutdown sequence, and its
contents are still lost on crash, same as older releases.

Bump PGSTAT_FILE_FORMAT_ID.

precedents_retrieved.title: Start WAL streaming as early as possible, without waiting for startup process to finish replaying existing WAL. This helps synchronous replication to resume quickly when significant replay lag has been built up.
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch starts the WAL receiver on a standby before the startup process finishes replaying WAL already in pg_wal, so synchronous commits on the primary are not held up by replay lag. A GUC, wal_receiver_start_condition, picks when the receiver starts, and the start LSN is the beginning of the most recently flushed segment, found by reading the first page of each segment in pg_wal.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Michael Paquier objected that the start LSN is roughly the consistency point, so streaming begins too early when many local segments, often copied by hand, are still left to replay. He also rejected the WAL page checks as hard to maintain, noted that the patch requests streaming when PrimaryConnInfo is not set, and suggested a WAL reader scan from the redo point to find the real end of local WAL. The entry stayed "Waiting on Author" after this review and was returned with feedback.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: Your patch would cause streaming to begin too early, and a manual copy of segments is not a rare thing as in some environments a bulk copy of segments can make the catchup of a standby faster than streaming.

precedents_retrieved.title: Eagerly evict bulkwrite strategy ring
precedents_retrieved.summary: Make the BAS_BULKWRITE buffer access strategy flush several dirty buffers in its ring at once, skipping buffers whose flush would require a WAL flush. This was meant as a first step toward combining writes and issuing them asynchronously, and gave about 15-20% faster parallel COPY FROM.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The author withdrew the entry after moving all of its patches into the patch set in the separate write combining thread, so the work continues there. No reviewer objected to the design; reviews found only code issues, which the author fixed. Earlier the author noted that the gain from this patch alone might not justify committing it.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: All of the patches that implement the bulkwrite eager flush functionality are included in the patch set being actively updated in this thread [1] on write combining.

precedents_retrieved.title: Backpatching injection point core facilities to REL_17_STABLE
precedents_retrieved.summary: Michael Paquier proposed backpatching core injection point APIs to REL_17_STABLE: cached points and loading for critical sections, IS_INJECTION_POINT_ATTACHED(), and runtime arguments. The goal was to make tests easier to port and to keep the facility consistent across stable branches, with v18 cherry-picks suggested later as a first step.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The visible messages do not show why. Tom Lane objected only to pushing such changes just before a release freeze and to touching v13, and Michael Paquier agreed. No later message records the withdrawal or its reason.

roaster_notes.note: P3 was recorded as returned because it stalled, so its reason does not carry over. P20 and P7 share only keywords or the hook mechanism and are not listed.
Three objections from the standards and compatibility angle.

The series adds no WAL records, no on-disk format change, no core catalog change and no protocol change. Only the hook placement on durable-state paths and the orphaned-ring lifecycle touch this angle.

From the security angle, the proposal has no gap that could support an objection. Capture defaults to off and is SUSET, with delegation through GRANT SET. Cross-backend reads of statistics and trace rings require pg_read_all_stats, which already sees more through pg_stat_activity and pg_stat_statements. The reset functions follow pg_signal_backend rules, and reset-all and the orphaned-ring sweep check superuser() in C. The orphaned-ring memory is bounded by ProcNumbers times ring size, and only a privileged setting can enable it. The hook contract is a safety concern for another angle, and these points need the code to confirm.
Two objections from this angle. Both concern where the collector lives and what it adds over existing tools; the hook design and its overhead are left to other angles.
Some demand exists: one consultant tested the patch and wants it, and the author describes real incidents. The material does not show demand beyond a few people or a lack of a workable external tool.
